title: Major Internal Organs
shortDescription: A dedicated organ-by-organ reference — heart, lungs, liver, stomach, intestines, pancreas, kidney, and brain — each with location, structure, function, and a high-yield fact.
genZNote: Small organs. Big responsibilities. This is the quick-reference chapter for all of them in one place.

illustration.alt: Labelled illustrations of the liver, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, pancreas, kidney, and brain, side by side
illustration.caption: Major Internal Organs — Cellfie Human Anatomy

structures.name: Liver
structures.description: Upper right abdomen; right and left lobes, dual blood supply (hepatic artery + portal vein).
structures.function: Produces bile, processes/stores nutrients, detoxifies blood.
structures.highYield: Receives blood from two sources: the hepatic artery (oxygen-rich) and the portal vein (nutrient-rich).

structures.name: Stomach
structures.description: Upper left abdomen; cardia, fundus, body, pylorus, with rugae (internal folds).
structures.function: Churns food with acid and enzymes to form chyme.
structures.highYield: Digests but does not absorb most nutrients — that's mainly the small intestine's job.

structures.name: Small intestine
structures.function: Main site of digestion and nutrient absorption in the GI tract.
structures.highYield: Villi and microvilli massively increase surface area for absorption.

image.alt: Labelled illustration of the small intestine

structures.name: Large intestine
structures.description: Cecum through rectum, with the appendix attached near the cecum.
structures.highYield: Absorbs water, not nutrients — nutrient absorption is mostly finished before material reaches it.

image.alt: Labelled illustration of the large intestine

structures.name: Pancreas
structures.description: Behind the stomach; head, body, tail, draining through the pancreatic duct.
structures.function: Dual role: exocrine (digestive enzymes) and endocrine (insulin/glucagon).
structures.highYield: Endocrine cells are clustered in the Islets of Langerhans.

structures.name: Kidney
structures.description: Renal cortex, renal medulla, renal pelvis; supplied by the renal artery, drained by the renal vein and ureter.
structures.function: Filters blood, maintains fluid/electrolyte balance, forms urine.
structures.highYield: The nephron, not the whole kidney, is the actual filtering unit — about a million per kidney.

structures.name: Brain
structures.description: Frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital lobes, plus cerebellum and brainstem.
structures.function: Reasoning, sensory processing, movement, vision, memory, and vital-function control, split across regions.
structures.highYield: The frontal lobe governs voluntary movement/reasoning; the occipital lobe governs vision.

comparisons.distinction: The liver produces bile; the gallbladder only stores and concentrates it (gallbladder is covered in the Digestive System chapter).
Small intestine absorbs nutrients; large intestine mainly absorbs water and forms stool — one of the most frequently tested pairings.
The stomach mainly digests (churns, adds acid/enzymes); the small intestine is where most actual nutrient absorption happens.

questions.prompt: In the labelled organ illustration, which organ has a dual blood supply from the hepatic artery and the portal vein?
questions.explanation: The liver uniquely receives blood from both the hepatic artery (oxygen-rich) and the portal vein (nutrient-rich, from the intestines).
optionNotes: Supplied by pancreatic vessels, not this dual system.
Supplied by the renal artery, a single main source.

questions.prompt: Which organ performs BOTH an exocrine (digestive enzyme) and an endocrine (hormone) function?
questions.explanation: The pancreas releases digestive enzymes into the small intestine (exocrine) and insulin/glucagon into the blood (endocrine) — two separate roles of one organ.
optionNotes: Has metabolic/bile roles, but not this specific exocrine+endocrine combination.
Filters blood and has some hormonal signaling, but not this classic dual exocrine/endocrine pairing.

questions.prompt: Which region of the brain is primarily responsible for processing vision?
questions.explanation: The occipital lobe, at the back of the brain, is primarily responsible for processing visual information.
optionNotes: Handles hearing, memory, and language comprehension.

questions.prompt: Which organ mainly absorbs water and forms stool, rather than absorbing nutrients?
questions.explanation: The large intestine mainly absorbs water and electrolytes and forms/stores stool; nutrient absorption is mostly finished in the small intestine before material reaches it.
optionNotes: This is the main nutrient-absorption site, not water-only.
Digests food, doesn't absorb water on this scale.
Neither absorbs water nor forms stool.

sections.heading: Liver
sections.body: Location: upper right side of the abdomen. Structure: divided into a right lobe and left lobe, supplied by the hepatic artery and portal vein, draining bile via the bile duct (which connects to the gallbladder).
bullets: Function — produces bile, processes and stores nutrients absorbed from the gut, detoxifies the blood.
High-yield fact — the liver receives blood from two sources: the hepatic artery (oxygen-rich) and the portal vein (nutrient-rich, from the intestines).
Common confusion — the liver produces bile; the gallbladder only stores and concentrates it.

sections.heading: Stomach
sections.body: Location: upper left abdomen, between the esophagus and small intestine. Structure: cardia (entry region), fundus (upper dome), body (main region), pylorus (exit region), with rugae (internal folds) that allow expansion.
bullets: Function — churns food and mixes it with acid and digestive enzymes to form chyme.
High-yield fact — stomach acid (hydrochloric acid) also kills many ingested pathogens.
Common confusion — the stomach digests but does not absorb most nutrients; that job belongs mainly to the small intestine.

sections.heading: Small Intestine
sections.body: Structure: three sections — duodenum (first, receives bile and pancreatic enzymes), jejunum (middle, main absorption site), ileum (last, absorbs remaining nutrients and vitamin B12).
bullets: Function — the main site of digestion and nutrient absorption in the entire GI tract.
High-yield fact — villi and microvilli lining the small intestine massively increase its surface area for absorption.
Common confusion — duodenum, jejunum, and ileum are three regions of one continuous organ, not three separate organs.

sections.heading: Large Intestine
sections.body: Structure: cecum → ascending colon → transverse colon → descending colon → sigmoid colon → rectum, with the appendix attached near the cecum.
bullets: Function — absorbs water and electrolytes from remaining digestive waste and forms/stores stool.
High-yield fact — the appendix has no confirmed essential digestive role in humans, though it may host beneficial gut bacteria.
Common confusion — the large intestine absorbs water, not nutrients — nutrient absorption is mostly finished by the time material reaches it.

sections.heading: Pancreas
sections.body: Location: behind the stomach. Structure: head, body, and tail, draining through the pancreatic duct.
bullets: Function — dual role: exocrine (digestive enzymes released into the small intestine) and endocrine (insulin and glucagon released into the blood).
High-yield fact — the endocrine cells of the pancreas are clustered in the Islets of Langerhans.
Common confusion — the pancreas' digestive-enzyme role and its blood-sugar-hormone role are two separate functions of the same organ, not the same process.

sections.heading: Kidney
sections.body: Structure: renal cortex (outer), renal medulla (inner), renal pelvis (collects urine), supplied by the renal artery and drained by the renal vein and ureter.
bullets: Function — filters waste from blood, maintains fluid and electrolyte balance, forms urine.
High-yield fact — the nephron, not the whole kidney, is the actual filtering unit; each kidney contains roughly a million nephrons.
Common confusion — see the dedicated Urinary System chapter for the full filtration process.

sections.heading: Brain
sections.body: Structure: frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital lobes of the cerebrum, plus the cerebellum and brainstem.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: This chapter is a single-page reference for seven major organs — liver, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, pancreas, kidney, and brain — each with location, structure, and function.
keyFacts: Liver: makes bile, processes nutrients, detoxifies blood. Gallbladder (not covered here) only stores bile.
Small intestine has three regions: duodenum, jejunum, ileum — main site of absorption.
Large intestine's job is water absorption and stool formation, not nutrient absorption.
Pancreas has both a digestive (enzymes) and hormonal (insulin/glucagon) function.
commonConfusion: Liver vs. gallbladder — production (liver) vs. storage (gallbladder) of bile.
Small intestine (absorbs nutrients) vs. large intestine (absorbs water) — a very commonly tested pairing.

highYieldFacts: The liver has a dual blood supply: hepatic artery (oxygen) and portal vein (nutrients from the gut).
The pancreas performs both exocrine (enzymes) and endocrine (hormones) functions.
The frontal lobe governs voluntary movement and reasoning; the occipital lobe governs vision.
commonTraps: Don't credit nutrient absorption to the large intestine — it mainly absorbs water.
Don't confuse the pancreas' two separate roles (digestive enzymes vs. blood-sugar hormones).
mustRemember: Eight organs covered: liver, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, pancreas, kidney, brain (plus heart and lungs from their own chapters).
